title: A bioinformatics pipeline for processing and analysis of whole transcriptome sequence data
author: Ayam Gupta

steps_raw.instruction:
A bioinformatics pipeline for processing and analysis of whole transcriptome sequence data
Ayam Gupta1, 3, Shalini Rajagopal1, 3,, Sonal Gupta1, 2, 4, Ashwani Kumar Mishra5 and Prashanth Suravajhala1, 6*
1Department of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics, Birla Institute of Scientific Research, Jaipur 302001,
Rajasthan, India; 2Department of Pediatrics, SMS Medical College and Hospital, Jaipur, Rajasthan, India;
3School of Biotechnology, Rajiv Gandhi Proudyogiki Vishwavidyalaya, State Technological University of
Madhya Pradesh, Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, India; 4Department of Biotechnology, Amity University Rajasthan,
Kant Kalwar, Jaipur 303002, India; 5DNA Xperts, Noida, India, 6Bioclues.org, India
*For correspondence: prash@bisr.res.in [Abstract]
Recent advances in next generation sequencing (NGS) technologies have paved the way for augmented genomic
research. From the conventional microarray analysis to the current NGS-based whole transcriptome pipelines,
there have been significant advances on how differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are identified. With several
bioinformatics pipelines in use, inferring the candidate DEGs prove to be a cumbersome approach as one may
have to reach consensus in analysing the results from various pipelines. To ensure this, we have benchmarked
the well-known Cufflinks-Cuffdiff pipeline on a set of datasets and present it in the form of a protocol for the
research community interested in performing downstream analysis of whole transcriptome shotgun sequencing.
Keywords: RNA-Seq, Transcriptome analysis, bioinformatics pipeline, differentially expressed genes [Background]
Whole transcriptome shotgun sequencing (WTSS or RNA-Seq) allows us to discover new genes and transcripts
and also measure their abundance in a single assay [1]. The quantitative expression of genes allows the
researchers in predicting the molecular mechanisms underlying genome regulation. High depth RNA-Seq tends
to be extremely sensitive allowing detection of lowly expressed transcripts when compared to microarray-based
quantification [2–4]. This quantitative measurement of gene expression enables researchers to characterize
transcripts from both coding and non-coding regions, identify abundances of RNA transcripts in diseased
individuals and predict molecular mechanisms underlying genome regulation. Several robust and sensitive
algorithms are available for the processing and analysis of RNA-Seq data. The protocols however vary based on
how good the publicly available datasets were used for an efficient benchmarking. In this protocol, we present a
bioinformatics workflow for quantitative analysis of RNA-Seq data and further compare it with publicly
available computational tools using different algorithms. Our pipeline uses open-source tools to process and
analyze RNA-Seq data starting with quality check until the last step of identification of differentially expressed
genes (see Software).

Dataset Information
For benchmarking, we have downloaded publicly available 1000 genome datasets
(http://www.internationalgenome.org/) with three different population accessions, viz. East Asian (ERR1050076
and ERR1050078), American (HG00731 and HG00733) and African ancestry (NA19238 and NA19240)
(Table1). Each population contains an individual as parent and child and type of RNA sequencing is strand
specific using Illumina platform. The files were downloaded either using FTP link or fasterq-dump
(https://www.internationalgenome.org/data-portal/sample) [5].

Procedure
The raw file (fastq) was processed using various steps which included quality check, alignment, sorting and
annotation. The pipeline uses a combination of various tools, viz. FastQC, Bowtie2/HISAT2, samtools, cufflinks
along with the human genome reference sequence (hg38 from UCSC human genome browser) and gene
coordinates information file (Figure 1). Since the commands in pipeline run on Linux, all commands are case
sensitive. This pipeline was run on a 64 GB RAM with 64 core CPUs in an Ubuntu operating system (16.04.4
LTS machine), but we recommend a minimum 16 GB RAM machine depending upon the raw fastq file size. A
shell script was created with extension .sh and all the commands are provided below. Figure 1: Flow chart for analysing RNA-Seq data.
A. Pre-processing of raw data
1. Quality check
The NGS analyses depend primarily on the raw data quality checks and so we used FastQC to plot the
read depth and quality score besides performing a host of other statistical inferences (Figure 2).
./FastQC ~/samples/sample1.fastq
# Command for quality check
Note: After a report is generated, several modules may be flagged as “Passed”, “Warn” or “Failed”.
But solely relying on the flags is highly discouraged as the statistics change with the type of input data. 4

Figure 2: Summary plots obtained from a standard FastQC run, containing information on statistics,
quality, read coverage, depth, yield, based per read call, etc From the FASTQC results, per sequence quality score plots the total number of reads vs the average
quality score over full length reads. The Phred score of above 25 is considered good wherein from the y
5

axis, the quality calls range from very good (green), the calls of reasonable quality (orange) can be
measured, while in pink, they are considered worse. The reads that fall in those regions could be
trimmed using cutadapt which is beyond the scope of this protocol. The distribution of average read
quality should be fairly tight in the upper range of the plot, whereas sequence content plot reports the
percent of bases called for each of the four nucleotides at each position across all reads in the file. Kmer
content plot measures the count of each short nucleotide of length k (default = 7) starting at each
position along the read.
2. Indexing human genome
Bowtie2 and HISAT2 were used to index reference genomes both of which work at high speed and are
memory efficient. Compared to Bowtie2, the Hisat2 indexing is more memory efficient although the
latter may skip intron-exon splice junctions.
./bowtie2 –build reference_inbt2_index_base
./hisat2 –build reference_inht2_index_base
#builds indices which are required for aligning reads
When the commands are run, Hisat2-build outputs a set of 8 files (with
suffixes .1.ht2, .2.ht2, .3.ht2, .4.ht2, .5.ht2, .6.ht2, .7.ht2, and .8.ht2). These files together constitute the
index: that is needed to align reads to that reference. The original sequence FASTA files are no longer
used by Hisat2, once the index is built. In case of Bowtie2, the current directory would contain six new
files that all start with reference and end with .1.bt2, .2.bt2, .3.bt2, .4.bt2, .rev.1.bt2, and .rev.2.bt2.
While the first four files are the forward strands, the rev files indicate the reverse indexed sequences in
case of Bowtie2.
3. Alignment and post processing
Hisat2 is a fast and sensitive alignment used to map RNA-Seq reads to the genome. Like Bowtie2,
Hisat2 also uses burrows-wheeler transform (BWT) to compress the genomes so that they require very
little memory to store. Unlike BWA and Bowtie, Hisat2 builds a whole genome global index and
thousands of small local indexes to make spliced alignment possible to run on a standard system in an
efficient way [6]. Bowtie2 is used for short read alignment and uses very little RAM with accuracy and
modest performance in indexing the alignment [7]. The mismatch or any sequencing errors or small
genetic variation between samples and reference genome could be checked using the following
commands:
./hisat2 –x reference_hisat_filename -1 path/filename1 -2 path/filename2 > filename.sam
./bowtie2 –x reference_filename -1 path/filename1 -2 path/filename2 > filename.sam
Note: The -2 option may be omitted for single-end sequences and –U may be used instead.
6

HISAT2 and Bowtie2 align a set of unpaired reads (in fastq or .fq format) to the reference genome
using the Ferragina and Manzini (FM) – index [7]. The alignment results output in SAM format [8] and
a short alignment summary is written to the console.
Samtools is a collection of tools to manipulate the resulting alignment in SAM/BAM format. SAM
stands for sequence alignment/map format and its corresponding format is binary mapped format
(BAM). SAM could be converted into different alignment format, sort, merge, alignment, remove
duplicates, call SNPs and short indel variants; whereas the BAM and following indices (.bai) are used to
view the index of the binary aligned sequences. The basic necessity of having the binary mapped files is
to save the memory.
./samtools import reference.fa ~/samples/sample1.sam > sample1.bam
4. Sorting BAM
A sorted BAM file is used for streamlined data processing to avoid extra alignment when loaded into
memory. Whereas it can be easily indexed for faster retrieval of alignment, overlapping is needed to
retrieve alignment from a region. All BAM files need to be sorted and indexed for better performance.
Samtools sort command is used to convert the BAM file to assorted BAM file and samtools index to
index BAM file.
~/samtools sort ~/samples/sample1.bam –o sample1.sorted
~/samtools index ~/samples/sample1.sorted
B. Examining differentially expressed genes
The Cufflinks suite of tools is used to perform a number of analyses for RNA-Seq experiments. It assembles
the transcripts and estimates their abundances, and finally examines differentially expressed genes (DEG) in
RNA-Seq samples. The Cufflinks suite includes several different programs that work together to perform
these analyses.
1. ./cufflinks in.sorted.bam –o sample.out
It is included in the Cufflinks package which helps in merging the assemblies. The merged assembly
provides us a basis for calculating genes and transcripts expression in each condition which are finally
analysed for DEGs through Cuffdiff command.
2. ./cuffmerge –g reference.gtf –s reference.fa sample.merged
Cuffmerge would merge all the replicate samples into one, while Cuffdiff compares the aligned reads from
RNA-Seq samples from two or more conditions and identifies transcripts that are differentially expressed
using a thorough statistical analysis, viz. the log2 fold change (log2FC) which is then reported as a set of
7

text files plotted graphically.
3. ./Cuffdiff ~/samples/sample1.out/transcripts.gtf ~/samples/sample1.sorted ~/samples/reference_genome
> sample_result
The current protocol is focused on the Cufflinks-Cuffdiff pipeline wherein the results are compared to the
already established DESeq2 pipeline using standard cutoff parameters. For the benchmarking process, two
different sequence aligners, i.e., Bowtie2 and Hisat2 were used for concision and comparison. Standard
cutoff parameters were considered for the analysis, i.e., log2FC and nominal p value < 0.05
Feature counts is a program for assigning mapping reads to genomic features such as genes, exons,
promoters and genomic bins [9].
Feature Counts –B –p –g gene_id –a ~/reference.gtf -o ~/sample.sorted.bam ~/sample.sorted.bam
DESeq2 is used for differential gene expression analysis based on the negative binomial distribution. It is a
Bioconductor package which is continually updated and available in R.
Data Analysis
1. Alignment of sequencing reads
Benchmarking yielded a good recovery rate for DEGs through RNA-Seq analysis. From six samples,
we obtained an RNA-Seq quality checked using FastQC. The reads were aligned to the human reference
genome assembly (hg38) that were downloaded from NCBI GenBank (ftp link) and then reaching
consensus with two aligning tools, viz. Bowtie2 and Hisat2. The average alignment percentage was
found to be 91.82% and 97.27% for Bowtie2 and Hisat2 respectively with the percentage of reads
mapped to the reference genome found to be similar between all six groups suggesting that there was no
sequencing bias in the data (Table2). Further from coverage percentage analysis between DESeq2
pipeline and the pipeline we used, this is observed as much lower than Bowtie2 (~90%) and Hisat2
(>90%) generated alignment files from our pipeline across all the samples (Figure 3) as unannotated
regions are also covered by it. The Bowtie2 and Hisat2 generated bam files were then used to generate
the read counts files for DESeq2 analysis.

2. Differentially expressed genes
The files were processed using cufflinks software with alternating the transcripts.outfile from both the
samples of the same population (Figure3). Cuffdiff analysis was done using transcripts.outfile (output
file from Cuffdiff) with parent:child as well as child:parent relationships which yielded diverse results.
9

We obtained an average of 272 (YRI), 356 (PUR) and 477 (CHS) DEGs using Cuffdiff taken as
parent:child and while taken as child:parent, we obtained an average of 214 (YRI), 358 (PUR) and 182
(CHS) DEGs. However, from the DeSeq2 pipeline, we obtained a higher number of average DEGs
among different populations as compared to our pipeline (Figure 3b and 3c). The up- and down
regulated gene counts obtained from the DeSeq2 pipeline in different populations were plotted in the
form of bar graphs (Figure 4) and Volcano plots, generated by comparing DEGs obtained from both
Bowtie2 and Hisat2 (Figure 5 and 6). While there is no general objective justification for any particular
log2FC threshold, from a mathematical point of view, it is possible to reject the null hypothesis at any
non-zero log2FC if the variability is low enough. We have set a log2FC and p-values and q-values <
0.05, as log2FC is robustly detected from RNA-Seq and qPCR. The DESeq2 code can be accessed via
https://github.com/ayamgupta/RNAseq_benchmark. Figure 4: Down-regulated and up-regulated gene count using the Cuffdiff and DESeq2 pipeline

Figure 6: From the downstream processing of files, 158 common genes were observed between the
Bowtie2- Cufflinks pipeline and Deseq2 in which 99 genes were observed to be common across Hisat2-
Cufflinks pipeline. A significant difference in the number of discovered DEGs was found in comparing the
Cufflinks-Cuffdiff pipeline when compared to DESeq2. These differences can be attributed to the coverage
of unannotated regions by the latter to some extent. Conclusions
Benchmarking is a gold standard for any NGS pipeline. It gives us inherent statistical interpretation on how
the data is used for further analyses. In this protocol, we have presented a RNA-Seq pipeline which can be
aptly used by beginners. While the Cufflinks-Cuffdiff pipeline is a simplest approach to identify the DEGs,
the tool such as DESeq is another alternative. It is unto the discretion of the end-user who should weigh the
approaches and finally reach consensus before analyzing the results. References
